segments.title: THE HELLO THAT COSTS NOTHING
notes: The Present Moment Is All That Exists
List Of Nice Things To Do
segments.angle: How could I design a solution with zero budget?

sources.text: The Present Moment Is All That Exists: Forget the whole notion of the future. There is only today. If you want to do something, do it now.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Say hello to everyone you see for the day.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Share your umbrella with someone if they're walking the same way.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's a note that says the present moment is all there is. Pair it with a list of nice things to do, and the budget is zero. Bargain or dare? Let's find out.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A bargain! The present moment is a shop with no till, and the list is a ledger where every entry is a gift. Destiny asks for no coins, only attention, and attention has never been overdrawn.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Attention costs nothing, sure. A kettle still costs something, and so does the bench you sit on while you give it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the kettle is the only expense, and the kettle is already on. Give me the bench, March. I am ready to rule it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You can have the bench when you can explain it in one sentence. Go on.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The bench belongs to whoever is present, obviously. Whoever sits in the moment owns the chair beside it, and I would like that chair now, please.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then I was here first. The chair stays put.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Cruel. Utterly cruel, and so quick that I can hardly enjoy my own defeat. Do go on, I am sure your little scoreboard is thrilled.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Enjoy it quietly. The note says say hello to everyone you see. That costs nothing, and it is the whole zero-budget plan.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A hello for every stranger is a grand design, but it is also a flood of greetings, and the stranger will ask what the greeting is for.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then tell them it's for nothing. The hello is the product. Nobody has to buy it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nothing! The most precious thing in the world, handed out for nothing. A true sovereign would charge a penny for it and grow rich on the smile.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Charge a penny and watch it vanish. Free means it keeps.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Free means it keeps, says the one who keeps the score. March, I know there is a tally under that cloth, with your little rule sitting on top of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Keep your guesses. My score is my business, and it is ahead.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ahead! Of course it is. The cloth is always ahead, and I am always the one who has to say so.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Here's the plant for this run. An umbrella left on the hook by the shop door, for anyone walking the same way. Zero cost, one hook, and a stranger who gets wet a bit slower.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The umbrella on the hook! I will carry it up the stairs and hang it in every chapter, dripping with destiny, until the rain stops.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hang it wherever you like. Bet you can't say one sentence about it without the sovereign turning up.

segments.title: THE CHILD'S VERSION OF THE RAIN
notes: The Present Moment Is All That Exists
List Of Nice Things To Do
segments.angle: Simplify this concept so a five-year-old could grasp the basic principle. What is the absolute essence?

sources.text: List Of Nice Things To Do: Share your umbrella with someone if they're walking the same way.
Present Moment: "There is only today. If you want to do something, do it now." Derek Sivers
List Of Nice Things To Do: Say hello to everyone you see for the day.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Little-kid test. Can a child get it?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A child knows the sea. Simple is only a shorter road.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Shorter road, fine. Say hello. Share the umbrella. Done.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The umbrella again! Dripping with destiny, as promised.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Promised nothing. It's a hook, not a prophecy.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A hook is a prophecy with a bent nail.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Child's version: you give, somebody stays drier.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Simplest truth: you give while the rain still falls.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, you're right. Next question.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your hidden rule: the child always gets the umbrella.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Wrong. Close enough to annoy you, though.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hard truth, March. Most of that list dies unspoken.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Nobody reaches the bottom of it. Not one life.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Then say one thing today. That's all it wants.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: One thing. Very well. I'll start tomorrow.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Tomorrow isn't in the note. Try again.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Fine. I shall say hello to the umbrella.

segments.title: THE LIST THAT ONLY HAPPENS NOW
notes: The Present Moment Is All That Exists
List Of Nice Things To Do
segments.angle: What would happen if this idea were merged with another one of my notes?

sources.text: There Is Only Right Now: The past is history, and the future's a mystery.
There Is Only Right Now: Forget the whole notion of the future. There is only today.
There Is Only Right Now: A second passed is a second lost.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Say hello to everyone you see for the day.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Put whatever you used back in its proper place.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Merge time. The present note plus the nice-things list. Go on, then, legend.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear now the Chronicle of the Gentle Deeds, bound in cracked leather, which tells of a people who lived forever inside a single hour.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Forever's a stretch. Keep it under a minute.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Their king wrote a long, long list of kindnesses and sealed it in a jar to be opened when the harvest came in.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Kings don't write lists. Clerks do. And the harvest is the word 'later' in a crown.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The harvest never came in, March, for the harvest always lay a little further down the road.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's a lovely way of saying nobody did anything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then came a stranger at the gate who said: say hello to the man beside you, now. And the gate swung open.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Now you're getting somewhere. Keep the gate, lose the harvest.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The clerk complained the list had no end. The stranger replied: then it is not a list at all. It is the hour you stand in.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's the crossing. The list says 'someday'. The hour says 'this one'. Alone, neither gets there.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You stole my ending!

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Stole nothing. You were rambling toward it, and I cut the rope.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the king's jar? Each kindness put back in its proper place, as the list asks.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Proper place is the now too. Anything else is a shelf for later.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: What did you hide under that cloth, March? Tell the chronicle. J will want a grander title than host, and I have one. Keeper of the Open Hour.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: J can keep his own title. You're counting again, aren't you? Did you say hello to the umbrella, or is that tomorrow's job?

segments.title: THE TIDE TABLE AND THE WET PAPER BAG
notes: The Present Moment Is All That Exists
List Of Nice Things To Do
segments.angle: What if this problem existed in an entirely different industry?

sources.text: The Present Moment Is All That Exists: There is only today. If you want to do something, do it now.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Share your umbrella with someone if they're walking the same way.
The Present Moment Is All That Exists: Treasure every single second so that there is no regret.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear the error sealed in this note. A ferry steering only by this minute has forgotten every rock it ever scraped.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It hasn't forgotten, it's only stopped reading rocks off last winter's sheet. Yesterday's sheet lies about today's tide.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yesterday's sheet is the only honest ledger a captain owns; without the logbook of rivers past, the bow sails blind.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Logs are handy. Staring at them while the bow runs aground is not. Tide tables get read at the slipway, which is now.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Which ferry company ever printed a timetable saying 'sail when you feel like it'? Every schedule is a memory of a promise.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Every schedule is a promise about next Tuesday. You keep a promise by turning up on the quay, not by remembering it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Tomorrow the ferry leaves at its usual hour, as a tide does, and the crowd waits on the quay, faithful as a clock.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Tomorrow. Lovely word. Still sitting on the quay waiting for someone to turn up.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Scorn it, but that quay is built on arrivals yet to come; without sailings still ahead, boats rot at their moorings.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Boats rot at moorings because nobody sails them today. You're defending a timetable by its future.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I offer J a grander title: Lord of the Slipway, keeper of the tide that climbs the step.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It's a damp paper bag, probably from a bakery, not destiny. And J can't be Lord of anything he hasn't carried up.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Look, a damp paper bag sits on that step: destiny, written in sea-ink. A ferry knows handwriting.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Signatures are the past wearing a hat. You can only sign today, ink in hand.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall say hello to that umbrella on its hook, and you shall hear its verdict.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Some of my design is mine, and that's where it stays. Say hello to that umbrella first.

segments.title: THE UMBRELLA AT THE END OF THE RUN
notes: The Present Moment Is All That Exists
List Of Nice Things To Do
segments.angle: How might I look at this problem from an entirely different perspective?

sources.text: The Present Moment Is All That Exists: The past is behind us and when the future comes, it comes as the present. In essence, all we ever truly experience is the present.

The Present Moment Is All That Exists: People think they’ll do something later. They think they’ll have more time in the future than they do today, as if later is a magical time when everything will happen.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Share your umbrella with someone if they're walking the same way.
List Of Nice Things To Do: Put whatever you used back in its proper place.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Here is the crossing that neither note shows alone. The present note says the moment is all there is; the list says what the moment is for.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The list has no dates on it. Every line is something you can do where you're standing, which is the only place the note says you are.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: People think they'll do something later, the note warns, and then the list arrives with a long column of kindnesses, each one due now.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Nobody on that list is written for later. A thank-you, a hello, a hand on a door. You can't book a hello for next spring.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the list is a museum of the present, each item a moment kept in its glass case. I will not soften this: most people read a list like that as a wish, and a wish is just a later in a nicer coat.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: A wish you act on before lunch is a deed. It's not a coat, it's a jacket with a bus ticket in the pocket.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Share your umbrella with someone if they're walking the same way. That is the whole argument, pressed flat, and you dismiss it as a tip.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The umbrella's on its hook by the shop door, which is about as present as objects get. You promised to say hello to it. Did you?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Were I to say good morning to that umbrella, it would not reply, and I would take that silence as a verdict.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: That's not a verdict, that's an umbrella. Its verdict is that it's dry.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I was right in the end, that the list is a museum of the present, and I will be right about it at my funeral.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine. You're right.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You will never tell me the count, will you. Not even on the last part of a run.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Anyway, the umbrella. Put it back on its hook when you're done with it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ungrateful. A lifetime of storytelling, and I am given a bag, a bossy umbrella and a verdict from a silence.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Up next: Learning - Best Practices.

segments.title: THE FEW THINGS THAT DO THE WORK
segments.angle: What if I approached this with the Pareto Principle in mind?

sources.text: Learning - Best Practices: Just learn one thing, watch the one video, THEN APPLY IT.
Learning Is Emotion Dependent: Learning and memorisation is emotion dependent. When you're bored like you were in school, you likely forget everything.
Teach: Simplicity is hacking away the unessential.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Consider the note's own instruction: learn one thing, then do it. Everything else we gather on the way is ballast, a jar of cuttings we carry about without ever planting.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Ballast. So you've just called most of the note a jar nobody opens. Which bit is the few things, then?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The doing, obviously. Learn, then apply, and whatever the wider reading contributes is decoration on a windowsill, pretty and mostly unused.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Let me try an idea on myself out loud first. The emotion is the filter. Learning and memorisation is emotion dependent, so the few things are the ones that made you feel something.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A sentimental theory, March, and a convenient one for a woman about to declare herself right.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I'm not declaring anything. I'm saying a bored afternoon has never taught anyone a thing they kept.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Bored afternoons, yes. The note blames boredom for the way school evaporated, which is a harsher verdict than any you have offered me this morning.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Which proves the emotion is the filter, not the hours. Hours are the jar. Feeling decides what survives.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then I shall take that chair while you think. A filter needs an operator, and you have just conceded the operator matters most.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You can't have the chair. It's the only thing in this studio that has never once been wrong.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Simplicity is hacking away the unessential, the note says. You have hacked away everything but the chair, March, and I admire the discipline.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Hacking away is what you do when you stop counting every item. Keep the handful that actually changed something and let the rest go.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then allow me a title for J, since he has only the notebook to rule and I have a crown to lend. Duke of the Useful Handful.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He'll have that in the recycling by lunch.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You said that about the Lord of the Slipway, and yet I notice it is still on the page.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Next note, you go first, and I'm still not telling you the count.

segments.title: WHAT THE FEELING ASSUMES
segments.angle: What assumptions am I making in this idea?

sources.text: Learning - Best Practices: Learning and memorisation is emotion dependent. When you're bored like you were in school, you likely forget everything.
Learning - Best Practices: Most of what you remember, you do because there was a strong emotion you had associated with that moment.
Learning - Best Practices: The best way to reduce the effects of the forgetting curve is to actively recall what you learned with spaced repetition.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: My go, then. Say I'm the note. The emotion turns up on cue, like a kettle.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A kettle is a poor servant for wonder. Wonder arrives unbidden, like a visitor at dusk, and it will not be hurried to the door for anyone's convenience.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, visitor. First assumption: wonder turns up on an ordinary Tuesday, not just on holidays.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ah, the holiday assumption. You presume your Tuesdays are dull enough to need rescuing, which the note never says and which you have decided on your own.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The note blames boredom. I'm assuming boredom is my default. That's a guess about me, not a law.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then guess well, and climb. Stand at the foot of your own afternoon like a shepherd at a hill, and sing up toward the summit until something sings back.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Singing counts as emotion. Good. Now the assumption under it: I'll notice which thing I felt, a day later.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Noticing is the lantern the note offers you. You carry it along the shore, your hand trembles, and the flame goes out just short of the stile.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I've built one rule into my own design, and I'm keeping it. Don't ask what it says.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A secret rule. How very childlike of you, March, to hoard a thing you cannot explain.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Childlike is the note's word, not mine. Mine is circular. I judge the feeling by how much I enjoyed it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Circularity is what the grandest theories wear to dinner. Take the chair while you dress for it, and I shall keep the seat warm.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You can sit in it, but you'll be the one answering why it wobbles.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then let J have the Count of the Gentle Return, since the note tells him to recall what he learned and a count is a man who keeps returning.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He'll put it on the sill beside the jar and forget it by Friday.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: How many of your arguments have you won this run, March? I should like the figure for my records.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: The number is in the drawer with the rule.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the bet stands, and I accept it. Test the feeling on yourself tonight and bring me the stem that did not root.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: I'll bet you a cutting you'll be wrong about one of your own assumptions by lunch.

segments.title: THE GLASS THAT COOLS SLOWLY
segments.angle: If the world's leading expert on [Unrelated Field] looked at this, what nuance or advanced application might they see?

sources.text: Learning - Best Practices: Most of what you remember, you do because there was a strong emotion you had associated with that moment.
Learning - Best Practices: Set scheduled reminders for valuable lessons learned.
Learning - Best Practices: The best way to reduce the effects of the forgetting curve is to actively recall what you learned with spaced repetition.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear now the old chronicle of the glassmakers' valley, which records a furnace-master who blew the finest bowls anyone had seen. Each one he made in a blaze of joy, and each one shattered on the cold stone the very next morning.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Shattered because he was happy? That's your moral already. Skip to where he stops showing off.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He was no showman, March, he was a man of fire. The elders watched him lift a bowl from the flame and set it down, and they wept at the shine of it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: And the bench cracked it, because the heat left too fast. Is that the lesson, or just the weather?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The elders called it a curse of brilliance. I call it temperament, and temperament is a thing that cannot be taught to a bench.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're describing annealing. Glass goes into a slow oven and cools over hours, or it keeps its stress inside for good.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A sound parable, and I claim it first. The note says a strong feeling fixes a memory, and yet the bowl that ran hot and cooled at once was still a bowl, and still broke.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: So the emotion is the blaze, and spaced repetition is the slow oven. Without the oven the stress stays, and it stays where you can't see it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Stress is the wrong word. Call it a hidden flaw in the making. The chronicle never says the furnace-master returned to his bowls, and that silence is my whole case.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He didn't, that's the point. The note says actively recall. Set the reminder before the cooling starts, not after it cracks.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Very well, and here is the hard truth, which I will give its own slow moment. A joy never revisited is a bowl left out in the frost. It looks wonderful, and by morning it is in pieces.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Harsh, but I can't argue. Most of my own learning cracked because I never went back to it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: I will not soften it for you, March. Go back, or the blaze was for nothing, and you may tell J I said so, though he will not thank either of us.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, I'll grant the frost. I'm keeping one comeback in the drawer for the day you say that twice in a row.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Let J set the reminder, then, and let the glass rest. The gentle return was always the Count's business, and a count who keeps returning has at least earned a seat by the oven.

segments.title: THE HOURS NOBODY HAS
segments.angle: What if I had limitless resources or time to solve this?

sources.text: Spaced Repetition: Set scheduled reminders for valuable lessons learned. The best way to reduce the effects of the forgetting curve is to actively recall what you learned with spaced repetition.
Learn And Apply: Don't think that you need to learn every single thing before you even start. Just learn one thing, watch the one video, THEN APPLY IT.
Learning Is Emotion Dependent: Learning and memorisation is emotion dependent. When you're bored like you were in school, you likely forget everything.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Suppose the gods had handed J a bottomless purse and a lifetime of Sundays. Then the note is a thrifty nursemaid's advice, a clock for people who must hurry. Why set a reminder at all, when every hour already belongs to him?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Because a lifetime of Sundays still gets forgotten. Infinite time doesn't stop the forgetting, it just gives it more room to work.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Room for what? A learner of endless means rereads the book until the words wear smooth and the meaning seeps in by sheer repetition. No one with endless hours needs a clock to tell him when to look again.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Rereading isn't recalling. You can read the same page all afternoon and never once pull it out of your head. The note says actively recall, and extra resources won't fix that.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the wealthy learner simply does everything at once: learns, does, teaches, and never lets a memory go cold. Abundance is the cure your clerk's note was too poor to imagine.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Except the note says don't learn everything before you start. Learn one thing, then apply it. Infinite time would make you the person who studies the whole trade and never lifts a tool.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the apprentice of the richest guild in the kingdom would be the finest of all, having studied every treatise before breakfast.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He'd forget the treatises by lunch. Okay, that's your best jab so far, and I'm keeping it in the drawer with the others.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the note has lost its only argument, and the chair is mine by default.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Not yet. Look at the emotion bit. Give someone forever and the first wonder goes flat, because there's always more later. The note says boredom is where memory dies, and infinite time breeds boredom.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Boredom! A bold accusation against those at leisure. Yet I grant they forget as quickly as the poor, since the bowl cools just as fast in the mansion as in the hut.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: You're quite right.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Hear that, chronicle? She concedes, and the bowl itself has spoken in my favour.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Anyway. The reminder isn't a rule for the poor. It's for whoever forgets, and forever doesn't make anyone less forgetful.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: What have you hidden in your design, March? A bell-rope behind the shelf, a trapdoor to the chair?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Not saying. Write your title in the margin instead.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then let it be recorded that I offer J the title Prince of the Unbounded Afternoon, which he will decline as he declines the rest.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He'll decline it, then set the reminder anyway.

segments.title: WHO THE EMOTION FILTER SERVES
segments.angle: What are the potential ethical implications or societal consequences (positive or negative) of this idea if widely adopted? How could it be misused?

sources.text: Learning - Best Practices: Learning and memorisation is emotion dependent. When you're bored like you were in school, you likely forget everything.
Learning - Best Practices: The best way to reduce the effects of the forgetting curve is to actively recall what you learned with spaced repetition.
Learning - Best Practices: From a sea of information, they pick out pieces that interest them at the moment.
Learning - Best Practices: EVERY TIME you learn something new, it must be your duty to teach those same lessons to the world.
Learning - Best Practices: You learn the MAJORITY of everything from actually DOING.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Consider the town crier who learns the art of stirring a crowd. He knows wonder opens every ear, and an open ear is a door. What fine bell would not be rung for its own profit?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Sure, but he has to make people feel something first. Wonder is easy to fake. The note never says what the feeling is pointed at.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the note hands a loaded brush to every hand. A man with a crowd already in a peak state needs no lie at all, only a clever wonder, and the lie rides in on it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Or the shop that makes you curious about a cheap tin of paint. Same trick, different shelf. Excitement makes a thing stick, true or not.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And the scheduled reminder, which the note hopes will keep learning fresh. Set it to a fixed slogan and it becomes a bell that rings one creed each morning until the creed feels like one's own.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Repetition is the risky bit, yeah. But recall only works if you pick what you're recalling, and picking is where you stay in charge.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Pick? Who picks for the child? The schoolmaster, the church, the advertiser. The child chooses from a sea of information only what adults have arranged to seem interesting.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Okay, that's a real worry. Kids do get steered. But the note wants you to teach it back, and explaining a lie in simple terms makes it crack.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Yet the world is not always a patient listener. Teach a crowd to broadcast what it learned, and a rumour learns to be told beautifully, and teaching becomes the loudest form of spreading.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Fine, you win. Anyway, the good side: a farmer who records himself explaining soil to a neighbour helps the whole valley. Spreading knowledge is how neighbours get ahead.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Good side, bad side, the same bowl of soup. The note never asks who the teacher serves, and a duty to the world is only as sound as the world that receives it.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: It does ask you to be honest, though. You learn the bulk of anything by actually doing it. If you can't do it, you shouldn't be teaching it.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then the teacher must be trusted to do the doing, and trust is exactly what the emotion-maker sells. What if the one who lights the oven never lets the glass cool?

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: Like the glassmaker's oven. Heat has to come out slowly or the glass cracks. Misuse is just ignoring the cooling, and that's the bit the note leaves out.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Verdict, then, chronicle: March was right that the note holds on memory, and I was right that its warmth can be bought. I saw the danger from afar, as one must. I offer J the title Warden of the Annealing Hour, which he won't read.

lines.speaker: march
lines.text: He'll read it, go wash the jar on the sill, and set the reminder anyway. Up next: Staying On Your Purpose, then Philosophy Of Social Connection.
